landscape.say: For businesses: Conference Room Privacy: Visual privacy for glass meeting rooms and partner offices, blocking sightlines to screens and whiteboards while daylight still reaches the room. Low-E: For older single-pane offices, schools and churches, a low-emissivity layer trimming summer heat gain and holding more heat indoors through DC winters. Office: Heat and glare control for perimeter offices from K Street to Tysons, installed after hours and floor by floor with landlord paperwork handled up front. Storefront: Display windows on corridors like M Street, Barracks Row and Bethesda Row stay visible to shoppers and run cooler under a light solar and UV film.

landscape.say: For homes: Security: Clear safety film for ground-floor windows, alley doors and basement units that holds broken glass in the frame and slows anyone trying to climb through. Glare Reduction: Film that tones down harsh light on home office monitors and TVs, including the glare bouncing off the Potomac and Anacostia into waterfront condos. Energy-Saving: Solar and low-E films that trim summer cooling and winter heating on older windows, a reversible upgrade where replacing historic sashes is difficult. Home Tinting: Window tinting for rowhouses, condos and suburban homes, planned room by room around front and rear exposures, with a clear, low-reflectance look that keeps historic district reviewers comfortable.

landscape.label: Why Window Film Here
landscape.title: Summer Heat, Humidity and Sun on Washington DC Glass
landscape.say: Washington summers are long, hot and sticky. Heat builds from late May, humid stretches keep the nights warm, and the downtown blocks hold heat well into the evening. Winters are cold enough to matter, with freezing nights and the occasional snowstorm, so the glass is a heat problem for half the year and a heat loss problem for much of the other half.

landscape.label: Local Know-How
landscape.title: Rowhouses, Historic Districts and Home Window Tinting in DC
landscape.say: Residential work here usually means a rowhouse. Federal-era houses in Georgetown, Victorian bay fronts on Capitol Hill and around Logan Circle, and converted townhouse condos in Dupont Circle all have the same quirks: windows only at the front and back, tall sashes, old glass that owners want to keep, and English basement units with windows at sidewalk level.

landscape.say: Common questions: Does film affect the warranty on my windows? Certain manufacturers of insulated glass restrict coverage once aftermarket film goes on. What drives the price of window film in DC? Four things: the film you pick, total square feet, the count of individual panes, and whether they need ladders, lifts or after-hours access. Do I need historic district approval to tint windows in Georgetown or on Capitol Hill? Interior film that keeps the glass looking clear is generally treated as a minor matter, but rules differ between Georgetown, which falls under the Commission of Fine Arts, and districts reviewed by the DC Historic Preservation Office.

landscape.say: Here's how an install works. First, start with the quote form: the address, approximate window sizes and the problem you want solved. Then, they confirm measurements, identify single-pane, insulated or low-E glass, and tape samples to the windows at the time of day the problem is worst. On install day, homes are usually done in a day. Finally, film needs time to dry fully, longer in humid summer weeks and cold winter months.
